HEBR0200.name: Elementary Hebrew
HEBR0200.description: This is the second half of a year-long course, an introduction to the skills of reading, writing, and conversing in contemporary Israeli Hebrew. Students also read Hebrew texts adapted for their level of Hebrew based on biblical, rabbinic, and modern Hebrew literature, which introduce them to the approaches of Hebrew writers in various periods and to a variety of cultural issues. Prerequisite: HEBR 0100. Students must have taken HEBR 0100 for credit to receive credit for this course. Exceptions must be approved by both the academic department and the Committee on Academic Standing. Enrollment limited to 20.

HEBR0400.name: Intermediate Hebrew
HEBR0400.description: Develops the skills of reading, writing, and conversing in contemporary Israeli Hebrew at the intermediate level and of reading Hebrew texts of the biblical, rabbinic, and modern periods (biblical stories, rabbinic legends, modern Hebrew poems, stories, essays, newspaper articles). Discussions and compositions focus on the psychological, cultural, political, and social issues reflected in the Hebrew sources that we study. Prerequisite: HEBR 0300 or equivalent. Enrollment limited to 20. If unable to enroll because of closed registration please contact the professor and a wait list will be created.

HIAA0076.name: From Turtle Island to Abya Yala: Art of the Indigenous Americas
HIAA0076.description: Before the western hemisphere was named after Amerigo Vespucci, it had many names, including “Turtle Island” and “Abya Yala.” Many people populated the Americas, from the Arctic and Pacific Northwest to the tip of Tierra del Fuego. These societies tracked days and seasons using complex calendrical systems, developed sophisticated philosophies about humankind’s relationship to nature, and created buildings, cities, monuments, and precious objects that continue to impress viewers today. This course introduces students to key aspects of the Indigenous art and architecture of this hemisphere, from their ancient origins to modern revitalizations and innovations. Over the semester, students will learn the names, characteristics, and key artistic accomplishments of the civilizations that populated the western half of the world.

HIAA0090.name: The Other History of Modern Architecture
HIAA0090.description: This lecture course presents modern architecture as the product of the cultural, technological, political, and intellectual developments associated with capitalist expansion across the globe. By exploring the trans-Atlantic slave trade and its effects on Western industrialization, European Jesuit gardeners in China, modernization efforts in 19th century Turkey and Japan, and tropical climate and colonial policy in India, Nigeria, and other global sites; the course will expose students to the “99 percent” who are frequently excluded from discussions about modern architecture, but whose labor and cultural traditions were crucial to the heroic modernism of the West.

HIAA0100.name: Introduction to Architectural Design Studio
HIAA0100.description: The class introduces students to basic tools and strategies in architectural design. A warmup exercise and several design assignments guide students to explore questions about form, function, structure, and light. The semester is devoted to the design of a small house. Students are trained in rigorous, conceptual thinking and graphically and verbally clear pronunciation of consequential design logic. By the end of the semester, the proposed building design is presented in concept diagrams, plans, sections, elevations, and a model. Course is intended for first and second year students. Preference is given to actual and future architecture concentrators. To apply for this class, students are required to submit an override request and a note via CAB to specify their concentration, semester level, and previous applications for this class.  Enrollment limited to 15.

HIAA0130.name: Architectural Projection
HIAA0130.description: This course introduces the beginning student to the origins, media, geometries and role(s) of projection drawing in the design and construction process. The student will learn systems of projection drawing from direct experience, and be challenged to work both from life and to life. Subjects such as transparency, figure/ground, sciagraphy, oblique projection, surface development, volumetric intersections, spatial manipulation and analytic operations will build on the basics of orthographic and conic projection. The course involves line and tone drawing, hand drafting, computer drawing(Autocad) and computer modeling(Rhino).

HIAA0405.name: Arts of the Sacred and the Demonic in the Ancient Mediterranean
HIAA0405.description: From rural temple to urban shrine, to elegant synagogue or village church, from household prayer nook to adorned tomb, people in the ancient world honored, encountered, and experienced their gods. They practiced a piety in which human flourishing depended on gestures, rituals, and built articulations of devotion mediated by beauty. But holy powers could also be malevolent, so ancient art served to protect, warn, or ward off evil spirits. This course will explore the art, architecture, and material cultures of ancient Greeks, Romans, Jews, and Christians between the 6th century BCE and the 6th century CE. We will consider a wide variety of evidence, including texts, sculpture, frescoes, mosaics, architecture, and domestic artifacts, to explore the many ways in which these distinct but connected communities expressed their beliefs through visual representations and material practices. A

HIAA0420.name: Cathedrals and Castles
HIAA0420.description: The course aims to engage critically with the major architectural features of the medieval world:  the cathedral and the castle.  In addition to examining specific buildings as case studies, we will also interrogate the cultural context and the material culture associated with the construction, use and meanings of these important spaces. The course is arranged thematically rather than chronologically. A

HIAA1190.name: Spaces and Institutions of Modernity
HIAA1190.description: This undergraduate seminar will explore canonical and emerging theories of modernity as they intersect with our understanding of space and the role of the built environment and designed objects within it. The seminar will be organized as a series of case studies of the iconic sites and institutions of modernity (the metropolis, the world's fair, the museum, the prison) as well as others that have also come to exemplify it (the ship, the plantation, the railroad, the colony). Class time will include analysis of primary documents and field trips to local sites.

HIAA1403.name: Finding Florence Day: Histories of the Fragment
HIAA1403.description: Florence E. Day (born 1908) was a scholar, curator, and the first person to receive a PhD in Islamic art history in the US. Through a twist of fate, her small but significant personal collection of historical material from the Islamic world came to Providence and is now divided between Brown's Joukowsky Institute (ceramics/ other media) and the RISD Museum (textiles). Day had no permanent institutional affiliation and left no personal archive, although there are traces to be found of her life and the frictions she encountered within her field of study. This object-focused seminar will explore Day’s collection and the methodologies that art historians, archaeologists, and historians can use to make meaning from a range of materials in a personal collection, asking how we tell the histories of objects -and a life - that now exist only in fragments.

HIAA1920.name: Individual Study Project in the History of Art and Architecture
HIAA1920.description: Reading and reports on an approved topic, supervised by a member of the staff. Project proposals must be submitted and approved no later than the first week of the semester. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

HIAA1990.name: Honors Thesis
HIAA1990.description: The subject of the thesis and program of study will be determined by the needs of the individual student. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

HIAA1992B.name: Honors Thesis Workshop
HIAA1992B.description: The Honors Thesis Workshop is a two-semester workshop (offered in the fall and spring semesters) for students who are writing an Honors Thesis in the History of Art and Architecture, and Architecture. Students taking the Workshop must also register for HIAA 1990 Honors Thesis with their advisor. This workshop supplements work with the advisor by supporting students in research and writing methods, bibliographic practice, archival strategies, and oral presentations. As a cohort, students will do peer reviews and respond to supportive feedback on their thesis. The workshop meets every week as a group on Tuesday; the Thursday class time is reserved for meeting individually with the Honors Thesis Workshop professor and for students to workshop their materials with peers. Students will complete a draft by the end of the fall, and present a final thesis in spring.

HIAA2403.name: Finding Florence Day: Histories of the Fragment
HIAA2403.description: Florence E. Day (born 1908) was a scholar, curator, and the first person to receive a PhD in Islamic art history in the US. Through a twist of fate, her small but significant personal collection of historical material from the Islamic world came to Providence and is now divided between Brown's Joukowsky Institute (ceramics/ other media) and the RISD Museum (textiles). Day had no permanent institutional affiliation and left no personal archive, although there are traces to be found of her life and the frictions she encountered within her field of study. This object-focused seminar will explore Day’s collection and the methodologies that art historians, archaeologists, and historians can use to make meaning from a range of materials in a personal collection, asking how we tell the histories of objects - and a life - that exist only in fragments.

HIAA2785.name: The Cultivation of Taste: Aesthetics and the Senses
HIAA2785.description: The study, criticism, and judgment of art is founded on a discourse around taste. How do we judge the merits of a work of art, whether it is good, bad, beautiful, ugly, or something else? Are aesthetic judgments universal, or subjective? Can individuals be trained in aesthetic systems to connect their own sensory experiences with other people’s encounters? How might taste distinguish people, separating them into different groups, as well as bring others together? What is the relationship between gustatory and aesthetic taste? In this class, we will focus on the writings of artists, philosophers, art critics, art historians, gastronomists, literary historians, anthropologists, and sociologists, from the eighteenth to the twentieth century, to trace a history of taste in Europe and Asia.

HIAA2871.name: Aesthetics and Embodiment in the Age of Artificiality
HIAA2871.description: This seminar will examine how notions of embodiment and aesthetic experience have been reshaped with the development of artificial intelligence since the 1950s. Our focus will be on the shifting political claims made about the entanglement of bodies and machines. Topics will include mechanical models of perception, machinic metaphors for experience, notions of dispersed intelligence, decentered subjects, embodied minds, cyborgs, surrogates, avatars, and affectivity. Our inquiry will be interdisciplinary and comparative, with an emphasis on how agency, experience, and meaning come to be understood at the intersection of technology and subjectivity.

HISP0200.name: Basic Spanish
HISP0200.description: A continuation of HISP 0100, focusing on acquisition of communicative skills (speaking, listening comprehension, reading, writing) as well as cultural awareness. With successful completion of the course students can carry on short spontaneous conversations and comprehend and produce simple texts involving everyday topics (such as modern day life and its pressures, health, art and culture, nature and the environment, relationships) with good command of grammar and sentence structure. Individual work outside of class (averaging one hour/day) prepares students for in-class activities focused on authentic communication. An additional conversation section (one hour/week) is required. Placement: HISP 0100, Brown placement score of 281 - 380. Students should check Placement/Course Description in the Undergraduate Program section of the Hispanic Studies website. Enrollment limited to 15; 12 spaces available during pre-registration, 3 additional spaces available at the start of the semester.

HISP0300.name: Intermediate Spanish I
HISP0300.description: This course carries on the work initiated in HISP0100-0200 to develop and strengthen students' linguistic, communicative, academic, and multicultural competencies through content- and language- integrated instruction. This course is framed by an inclusive perspective on learning and embraces diverse identities and communities in the Hispanic World. It offers a variety of texts, themes, and topics related to students’ academic and life experiences, while also helping them develop professional skills. An additional conversation section (one hour/week) is required. Prerequisites: HISP 0200. Brown placement score: 381-460. Students should check Placement and Course Description in the Undergraduate Program section of the Hispanic Studies Website. Enrollment limited to 15; 12 spaces are available during pre-registration, 3 additional spaces available at the start of the semester.

HISP0400.name: Intermediate Spanish II
HISP0400.description: A continuation of HISP 0300. This course continues to strengthen students’ linguistic, communicative, and multicultural competencies through content- and language- integrated instruction. Students engage with a variety of social, cultural, and personal themes, using language in meaningful, real-world contexts. Emphasis is placed on active engagement, collaborative projects, and interactive activities that enhance both language proficiency and cultural awareness. An additional conversation section (one hour/week) is required. Prerequisites: HISP 0300, Brown placement score: 461-540. Students should check Placement and Course Description in the Undergraduate Program section of the Hispanic Studies Website. Enrollment limited to 15; 12 spaces are available during pre-registration, 3 additional spaces available at the start of the semester.

HISP0500C.name: Advanced Spanish: Vivir la ciudad City Lives, Urban Communities
HISP0500C.description: Courses at the 500 level advance students’ Spanish language skills through engagement with a wide range of authentic materials (literary and non-fiction texts, film, podcasts, and more), preparatory individual work for class discussion, and projects completed outside of class, while expanding and refining their knowledge of the Spanish language system. Cities are home to more than 80% of Latin America and Spain’s population. In HISP0500C we explore their rich human and cultural landscapes, examining opportunities and challenges of urban life in the Spanish-speaking world, including Latinx communities in the US. An additional conversation section (one hour/week) is required. HISP 0400, Brown placement test score 541-650. Check Placement and Course Description in the Undergraduate Program section of the Hispanic Studies website. Enrollment limited to 15; 12 spaces available during pre-registration, 3 additional spaces available at start of semester.

HISP0630F.name: Narrating Food, Tasting Words: A Culinary Adventure through Hispanic & Lusophone Worlds
HISP0630F.description: This course explores cultural representations of local, regional, and national culinary traditions in the Spanish-speaking world. Drawing on music, film, television series, poetry, fiction, and visual art, we will explore how food and food culture reflects, creates, maps, and projects countries and regions from Spain to Latin America locally, nationally, and internationally. We will also examine connections between food and the environment and diet and class, as well as other aspects of identity manifested in eating habits. In addition to our weekly meetings, we will come together every 3-4 weeks to prepare a class meal based on regional cuisines. This course focuses on creating: from a class recipe book to creative and academic projects. The class will be taught in Spanish with elements of Portuguese, English, African, Indigenous, and other cultural traditions tied to the cuisines of the Spanish-speaking world.

HISP0650.name: Advanced Spanish Through Literature & Film
HISP0650.description: HISP 0650 studies literature and film from Latin America and Spain through critical reading and analytical writing. The course serves as an introduction to the literatures and cultures of the Spanish-speaking world, covering a range of periods and genres (e.g. the short story, the novel, poetry, theater, film, and non-fiction). Beyond offering a historical and contextualized panorama of cultural production from the Spanish-speaking world, HISP 0650 will also help you develop new strategies for reading, writing, and thinking about literature and film, preparing you for more advanced literature and culture courses at the 1000 level. Placement: Two HISP courses at the 500 level; HISP 600; or Brown Placement test score of 651 or above.

HISP0650B.name: Con estilo y buena gramática: Advanced Spanish Writing
HISP0650B.description: This advanced Spanish course is designed for students who wish to hone their spoken and written Spanish language. Organized in thematic blocks, students will review complex Spanish grammar and syntax, learn how to structure and compose diverse types of essays and other genres of writing (including documents geared toward professionalization, such as e-mails or cover letters), and participate in different real-life situations to improve their spoken skills. Engaging with texts and visual culture across different genres, students will learn new vocabulary as well as learn about the art, culture, and literature from the Spanish-speaking world. By the end of the semester students will master advanced Spanish grammar, syntax, and techniques of composition in order to produce –without the need of generative AI– good writing in Spanish.

HISP0730.name: Encounters: Latin America in Its Literature and Culture
HISP0730.description: An introduction to major authors, movements, and themes of Spanish American literature from the Discovery to the present. This course also aims to develop students' oral and written expression in Spanish. Students are expected to engage in close reading and discussion of texts, as well as to revise their papers. Prerequisite: HISP 0600, or AP score =5, or SAT II (Literature) score of 750 or above, or Brown placement score of 651 or above.

HISP0900T.name: Introduction to Professional Translation and Interpretation
HISP0900T.description: What is translation? Interpretation? What roles do the translator and interpreter play in communication? What skills and kinds of knowledge are needed to develop competency in translation and interpretation as professional/community services? What factors shape how a text is translated (e.g., purpose, intended audience, type and genre, intercultural differences)? What is the role of translation in advancing language competence and proficiency? Through a functionalist approach, students advance their mastery of Spanish and develop translation competence. In addition to academic work (readings, translation assignments, and in-class exercises), students will also gain practical experience working with Spanish-speaking clinics and community organizations.

HISP1330Z.name: Tropical Fictions: Geography and Literature in Latin American Culture
HISP1330Z.description: Tropical nature in Latin America has been represented in conflicting ways: a place of leisure and sensuality, but also of depravity and sloth; a place of infinite riches but also a space where disease and racial degeneration thrive. Tracing the variations and endurances of these tropes in 18th- to 21st-century Western consciousness, this course aims to re-think the tropics in literature, film and the arts from a vantage point different to that of temperate-climate European civilization. Readings include canonical fictions such as La vorágine (1924), 19th-century European travelogues from the region, as well as contemporary indigenous art.

HISP2160R.name: Authorship and Authority in Early Modern Spain
HISP2160R.description: This seminar offers a panoramic view of early modern Spanish literature and book history through the study of both canonical and less frequently read works. With a focus on questions of authorship and authority, we will read poetry, prose, and drama in relation to the material and social conditions of their production and reception, considering how competing arenas of patronage, the emergence of a commercial market for books and plays, and, perhaps paradoxically, legal and ideological constraints helped shape a literary culture of exceptional productivity and inventiveness whose influence extended across Europe and into the Americas.

HISP2250Q.name: Las nuestras: narradoras latinoamericanas del siglo XXI
HISP2250Q.description:
Centering women’s writing as a key site of aesthetic and political experimentation, this course examines twenty-first-century Latin American literature from a comparative, cross-regional perspective across Spanish-speaking contexts and diasporas. Through novels, short stories, and essays, we explore how established and emerging writers engage gender, race, indignity, inequality, territory, and ecology as intertwined terrains of literary creation and intervention. Drawing on feminist, transfeminist, decolonial, speculative, and multispecies frameworks, the
course approaches literature as a critical and disruptive practice that unsettles male-dominant canons, interrogates regimes of value and recognition, and generates situated, affective, and theoretically engaged modes of storytelling and critical inquiry.

HISP2990B.name: Proseminar in Hispanic Studies
HISP2990B.description: This proseminar’s aims are twofold: 1) to provide graduate students with a map of the discipline of Hispanic Studies, with attention to its history and to its newest directions; and 2) to demystify key elements of an academic career, both specific to the doctoral program in our department and more generally. The bulk of course’s meetings will therefore have a dual structure. In the first half of our sessions, we will center on particular fields and their representative and innovative essays, in discussions introduced by members of the department and beyond. The second half of each class session will be devoted to practical issues around professionalization (article publication, reviews, conference participation, crafting the dissertation, etc.). Students will be closely involved in the planning of the course, contributing suggestions for topics to explore and potentially presenting samples of their own work.

HIST0150D.name: Refugees: A Twentieth-Century History
HIST0150D.description:
Refugees are arguably the most important social, political and legal category of the twentieth century. This introductory lecture course locates the emergence of the figure of the refugee in histories of border-making, nation-state formation and political conflicts across the twentieth century to understand how displacement and humanitarianism came to be organized as international responses to forms of exclusion, war, disaster and inequality.
Syllabus link: https://blogs.brown.edu/refugees-20th-century/

HIST0150G.name: History of Law: Great Trials
HIST0150G.description: Through discussion of a variety of trials spanning more than two millennia, this course will probe the nature of demonstrative and transitional justice, the relationship between ideology and law in different societies and time periods, and how trials affirm or contest legal personhood, criminal responsibility, and social marginalization. Cases to be covered include: Socrates, Jesus Christ, the French Revolutionary Terror, the Amistad case, the Dreyfus Affair, the fictional Japanese Rashomon trial, the Stalinist show trials, the Nuremberg trials, and the trials of Nelson Mandela, O.J. Simpson, Dilma Rousseff, and Saddam Hussein (to name a few).

HIST0216.name: Southeast Asian History
HIST0216.description: From Melaka to Manila, and from sultanates to megacities, this new course introduces students to the plural past of Southeast Asia. In doing so, it analyzes how the region came to be (as a field of study in the mid-twentieth century), while surveying, too, the ways in which histories of polity, port, empire, and revolution have shaped not only the world in Southeast Asia—but also Southeast Asia in the world.

HIST0244.name: Understanding the Middle East: A Modern History
HIST0244.description: The Middle East is the only region of land to bridge three continents and is (arguably) the most controversial in America today. Assuming no prior knowledge of a region that persistently captures headlines, this course provides a robust academic introduction to modern Middle East history from the late Ottoman Empire to contemporary times. Throughout, we explore an amorphous but pivotal world region stretching from Algeria to Afghanistan, and Turkey to Yemen, via land, sea, air, and a variety of “3D” perspectives: from local environments and economies, to governance and geopolitics; language, kinship, and faith, to art, music, and sports. Most of all, we shall seek to understand how competing modern forces like constitutionalism, militarism, and humanitarianism; colonialism, nationalism, and international law; and elites to everyday people shape(d) the region today.

HIST0254.name: Reconstruction and the Politics of Violence
HIST0254.description: Examines Reconstruction (conventionally, 1863-1877, and often called the first civil rights revolution in the United States), and the political violence used to combat it.  The course places the events of this period in the broader American history of civil rights and the American penchant for political violence, with particular attention to antebellum mobbing, the Civil War, and Jim Crow lynching, but also looking at other forms of political violence such as Native American dispossession and labor unrest.

HIST0255A.name: Mexican American History
HIST0255A.description: This course provides a comprehensive historical examination of ethnic Mexicans in the United States. Students first address Native American societies prior to European colonization in order to understand the historical antecedents of Mexican people in the US. Proceeding chronologically, students then examine how the Spanish colonial era, Mexican Independence, and other major events during the nineteenth century shaped the “Mexican American” experience. We also explore the history of Mexican community in the U.S. during the American conquest of the Southwest, the twentieth century immigration experience, and the development of diverse Mexican American communities after 1900. By utilizing primary and secondary sources, we will explore major questions, theory, and research methods pertinent to Mexican American & Chicano/a/x history, including, immigration, xenophobia, ethnic identity formation, gender, articulations of race and labor in urban and rural settings, political activism, and urban cultures.

HIST0583A.name: Twins
HIST0583A.description: How and when have twins shaped history? How, in turn, have popular experiences and understandings of twins changed over time? This FYS will survey the historical significance of twins and multiples--famous and ordinary alike--with a particular focus on the modern period.

HIST0931D.name: Zionism: A History from the 19th Century to the Present (JUDS 0051)
HIST0931D.description: Interested students must register for JUDS 0051.

HIST1080.name: Humanitarianism and Conflict in Africa
HIST1080.description: This course focuses on the major issues and debates concerning humanitarianism and international intervention in 20th century Africa. It will explore the history of humanitarianism and the many challenges that arise when governments and institutions intervene in a conflict. Then students will investigate specific sites of conflict in Africa (ranging from Nigeria, Somalia, Rwanda, Sudan, and Western Sahara) and analyze different models of intervention and aid. These case studies will expose students to pivotal events in African history and equip them with a critical vocabulary with which to assess contemporary conflicts.

HIST1123.name: China's Socialist Dreams
HIST1123.description: A history of the People's Republic of China under Mao in its context. We’ll explore the appeal of anarchism and socialism in the early 20th century and experiments in rural utopianism and worker autonomy. To understand the Chinese Communist Party, we’ll examine it as upstart, revolutionary vanguard, strategic ally, army, and state builder. Using new research on 1950s-70s Chinese society, we’ll ask how the Maoist party-state reached the lives of urbanites and farmers; affected gender relations and constructions of sexuality, age, and family; and shifted formulations of ethnicity, race and China’s place in the world.

HIST1149.name: Imperial Japan
HIST1149.description: This course is for students interested in exploring the changing ideas, technologies and practices that shaped Japan’s history from the 1850s, when it confronted the power of an encroaching West, to the 1930s when its choices led the nation to the edge of ruin. Lectures and readings will address the collapse of the Tokugawa regime, the Meiji Restoration, the construction of empire, and the emergence of new forms of cultural and political expression. Students will also learn how ideas about gender, race, and tradition were understood and made use of in Imperial Japan. Open to all students.

HIST1211.name: Becoming Medieval: Self, Other, and the World
HIST1211.description: Complex relations among the foundational categories of self, other, and the world emerged in high medieval Europe that shaped the future of the globe. In exploring the high middle ages, this course exposes constructions of the self and patterns of power that engendered xenophobia, colonizing conquests, anti-Semitism, Islamophobia, environmental change, surveillance of deviants, and stark hierarchies of class, gender, and sexuality. Yet cross-dressing peasant girls who led armies, crusading knights who wore Muslim silks, Jews who advised Christian rulers, sub-Saharan Africans who enjoyed prominence at European courts, and Mongol-curious missionaries also belonged to the process of becoming medieval. As this course demonstrates, Europe in this period became intertwined with other regions, and was home to people of a diverse array of identities who lived boundary-defying lives and articulated capacious notions of self, other, and the world that resonate today.

HIST1457B.name: Understanding the Palestinians: 1948-present
HIST1457B.description: Palestinians are largely absent in histories of the “Arab-Israeli Conflict.” This course draws on new scholarship that centers Palestinian experiences from the Nakba (catastrophe) of 1948 to the present. We explore the social and cultural histories of all Palestinians –in Israel, in the Occupied Territories, and in the diaspora—and their struggles for equality, self-determination, and the right of return. Ultimately, we ask: what is the Palestinian condition? And why has it become a global signifier for imagining a just and shared world?

HIST1531B.name: Mass Movements, Modern Politics: From Labor to the New Right in America
HIST1531B.description: From the rise of the labor movement in the 1930s through the ascendancy of the New Right in the 1980s, this course considers how mass movements have shaped politics, lifeways, and culture in the twentieth-century United States. We explore how mass movements form, their structural and organizational character, their inclusions and exclusions, their intersection with identities, and their contestations with power. Topics include trade unions, feminisms, Black Freedom, racial nationalisms, anti-communism, and the New Left, among others. The course is fundamentally about how mass movements engaged with, and sought to transform, political culture in the modern United States.

HIST1554.name: American Empire Since 1890
HIST1554.description: This survey of twentieth-century US history through the lens of racial capitalism and empire will focus on the United States as a settler state whose power also relies on overseas colonialism and free trade imperialism. Topics include: ideology and political culture, labor and extraction, social movements and resistance, knowledge production and the military-industrial-complex, neoliberal scarcity and financialization.

HIST1641.name: South Asia through the Image Archive
HIST1641.description: In this course, we will look at some iconic paintings, photographs and films and interrogate the twentieth century as a century of decolonization through them.

HIST1820B.name: China's Environmental History
HIST1820B.description: As one of the world’s great civilizations, China has among the most thoroughly transformed environments on earth, and an abundant corpus of writing that shows how that transformation happened. This course will explore China's environmental history from the first farmers to the industrial present, examining how wildlife was eliminated by the spread of agriculture, how states colonized territory, how water systems were built and rebuilt, and how modern communism and capitalism have accelerated environmental change. We will approach China’s environmental history through a wide variety of translated sources from China, including philosophical texts, landscape poetry, medical manuals, travel narratives, legal statutes, Buddhist texts, recipe books, and science fiction. No prior background in Asian or environmental history is required.

HIST1930W.name: Introduction to Yiddish Culture (JUDS 1713)

HIST1931B.name: Money, Power, Sex and Love: the Modern Jewish Family in Europe and America (JUDS 1722)
HIST1931B.description: Interested students must register for JUDS 1722.

HIST1931F.name: Mediterranean Culture Wars: Archaic Greek History, c. 1200 to 479 BC (CLAS 1210).
HIST1931F.description: Interested students must register for CLAS 1210.

HIST1952B.name: The Intimate State: The Politics of Gender, Sex, and Family in the U.S.
HIST1952B.description: This seminar examines the “intimate politics” of gender, sexuality, and race in modern American history, focusing on law and political conflict from Reconstruction to the present. Its central concern is how the “private” (the intimate) is constructed and regulated by state power—by government. Topics include laws regulating sex and marriage; social norms governing gender roles in both private and public life; the range of political perspectives (from feminist to conservative) on sex, sexuality, and family; the transition from slavery to freedom; gender, sexuality, and U.S. empire; and the relationship of gender, sexuality, and race to notions of nationhood and the role of the modern state. Some background in history recommended but not required.

HIST1956A.name: Thinking Historically: A History of History Writing
HIST1956A.description: Philosopher George Santayana famously warned that “Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.” Ten years later, industrialist Henry Ford perhaps even more famously dismissed that notion: “History is more or less bunk.” What we mean by history and how we construct and use it are essential questions in all societies. Thinking Historically explores how we view and employ the past. The course examines major ways of interpreting the past through a survey of historians and methods and studies how history is produced, used, and misused, by professionals as well as by the public.

HIST1962H.name: Cities in Motion: A History of Urban Southeast Asia
HIST1962H.description: This capstone seminar explores how Southeast Asia became urban, from the commerce of early-modern entrepots such as Ayutthaya to the crisis of today’s sinking megacities like Manila, Bangkok, and Jakarta (the planet’s most populous: 42 million). Spanning fields and disciplines, it examines the arc and diversity of Southeast Asian urban history: asking why and in what ways has the rise of the city shaped the story of the region—and how has the story of the region shaped the life of the city. In working through these questions (and ecologies), the seminar draws on a mix of primary sources, visual archives, and scholarly analyses.

HIST1968A.name: Approaches to the Middle East
HIST1968A.description: When and why did the Middle East emerge as a field of study? What are the different approaches that frame our understanding of this pivotal region, and how did they change over time? This upper-level seminar explores these questions within the larger context of colonial and national and encounters that have shaped modern regimes of knowledge production. The class features visits by leading scholars from different disciplines who reflect on the questions they ask and how they go about answering them. Readings range from canonical works to innovative new scholarship. No pre-requisites but previous coursework on this region recommended.

HIST1970F.name: Early American and Atlantic Money
HIST1970F.description: The history of finance has become a crucial site for studying governance and statecraft, for recovering the organizing logic of capitalism, and for recognizing the structures of power in any given society. Topics include the recurring debates over metallic and paper currencies, the emergence of a national banking systems, and the technologies of coinage, assaying, and counterfeiting. Particular focus on the relationship among finance, colonization, and slavery, as well as the many speculative monetary systems that circled around the Atlantic world from the fifteenth century through the nineteenth century.

HIST1972N.name: Archiving Ideology and Power
HIST1972N.description: This U.S. history research seminar introduces students to the Brown University Library’s Special Collections and assists Special Collections by having students locate and collect primary sources to extend and complement the Gordon Hall and Grace Hoag Collection of Dissenting and Extremist Printed Propaganda. The Hall-Hoag is an enormous collection of largely Cold War-era pamphlets, leaflets, newsletters, funding and base-building literature and other materials by U.S. activist groups. The groups range from the far left (e.g., Black Panthers) to the far right (e.g., Neo-Nazis), as well as moderates (e.g., National Organization of Women or NOW). We will learn about archival practices and attempts to give voice to those who have been traditionally silenced through oral history, as well as documentation of texts and other material objects.

HIST1974P.name: Modernity's Crisis: Jewish History from the French Revolution to the Election of Donald Trump
HIST1974P.description: As the modern world developed and grew, the question of the Jews’ place within it became increasingly important for the majority societies and the Jews themselves to deal with.  The solutions found have ranged from inclusion on equal terms through exclusion not only from society but from humanity altogether.  In many ways, the debates around this issue have touched on the very meaning of modernity itself.  In this advanced undergraduate seminar, we will examine the ongoing polemics on the place of the Jews from the perspectives of both the proponents of the different solutions and the Jews themselves.

HIST1976K.name: The Invention of Nature: Enlightenment Natural Histories
HIST1976K.description: From butterflies and caterpillars to indigo and sugar cane, the natural world exploded in the eighteenth century onto the pages of books, maps, and manuscripts, rewriting nature and history on a planetary scale. This course brings students into contact with this reinvented world of nature through the extraordinary collection of the John Carter Brown Library, one of the leading special collections libraries with a spectacular repository of books related to the natural history of an expanding globe. From the colorful pages of Maria Sibylla Merian to the florid descriptions of Alexander von Humboldt, we will explore materials from Brazil, Mexico, the Caribbean, and far beyond, with the goal of understanding how early modern naturalists and travelers imagined these colonial spaces and described their environments and inhabitants – animal, vegetable, mineral, and human – for all the world to see.

HIST1990.description: Guided reading on selected topics. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

HIST1992.name: History Honors Workshop for Prospective Thesis Writers
HIST1992.description: Prospective honors students are encouraged to enroll in HIST 1992 during semesters 5 or 6. HIST 1992 offers a consideration of historical methodology and techniques of writing and research with the goal of preparing to write a senior thesis in history.  The course helps students refine research skills, define a project,  and prepare a thesis prospectus, which is required for admission to honors. Students who complete honors may count HIST 1992 as a concentration requirement. Limited to juniors who qualify for the honors program.

HIST1993.name: History Honors Workshop for Thesis Writers, Part I
HIST1993.description: All students admitted to the History Honors Program must enroll in HIST 1993 for two semesters of thesis research and writing. They may enroll in the course during semesters 6 and 7, or 7 and 8. Course work entails researching, organizing, writing a history honors thesis. Presentation of work and critique of peers' work required. Limited to seniors and juniors who have been admitted to History Honors Program. HIST 1993 is a mandatory S/NC course. See History Concentration Honors Requirements.

HIST1994.name: History Honors Workshop for Thesis Writers, Part II
HIST1994.description: This is the second half of a year-long course, upon completion the grade will revert to HIST 1993. Prerequisite: HIST 1993.

HIST2890.name: Preliminary Examination Preparation
HIST2890.description: For graduate students who have met the tuition requirement and are paying the registration fee to continue active enrollment while preparing for a preliminary examination.

HIST2910.name: Reading and Research
HIST2910.description: Section numbers vary by instructor. Please see check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

HIST2930.name: The Roots of History
HIST2930.description: “The Roots of History” encourages critical thinking about some of the different ways in which historians approach thinking and writing about the past. In particular, we will explore some of the major theoretical stances that have influenced the discipline of history. Our focus throughout will be the interplay between theory and practice. By examining how historians have grappled with questions posed by influential thinkers (often working within other fields of knowledge), we will chart the trajectory of the discipline and assess its working methods. Required for all first-year PhD students in History.

HIST2960.name: Prospectus Development Seminar
HIST2960.description: This collaborative seminar focuses on identifying and contextualizing a dissertation topic; choosing a dissertation committee and a support network; designing and executing plans for research and writing; and articulating a thesis project as a prospectus, grant proposal, and other oral and written forms. This is a required course for and open only to third-year students in the History Ph.D. program.

HIST2970Q.name: Core Readings in 20th Century United States History
HIST2970Q.description: This graduate readings course offers an intensive exploration of major themes, problems, and scholarly interpretations in 20th-century United States history. Through extensive reading of key historical monographs, articles, and primary documents, students will trace the nation's trajectory from the Progressive Era through the complexities of the post-Cold War era and into the 21st century. Key themes include race, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, religion, politics, and foreign policy.

HIST2971I.name: New Perspectives on Medieval History
HIST2971I.description: Over the past several decades, the field of medieval history has been reshaped radically. New approaches have changed the ways in which medievalists think about old subjects. Our understanding of medieval society itself has expanded as previously marginalized or unexplored subjects have become central to medievalists’ concerns. This seminar explores the ways in which medievalist historians have altered how they practice their craft in response to these developments. Readings in classic older works are juxtaposed with newer ones on the way to becoming classics themselves.

HIST2982D.name: The Three Ages of Antisemitism
HIST2982D.description: This graduate seminar will examine the history and historiography of antisemitism in three geopolitical and discursive chapters. We will begin with the anti-Judaism that developed in the early Christian era in the Middle East and Mediterranean and continued in European and Islamic contexts. We will continue with the largely European, 19th-century evolution of modern antisemitism and its scientific and racializing claims. Finally, we will look at the contemporary political and ideological uses of antisemitism accusations, including its imbrications within the Israel/Palestine conflict.

HIST2990.name: Thesis Preparation
HIST2990.description: For graduate students who have met the residency requirement and are continuing research on a full time basis.

HIST2991.name: History Dissertation Writing Workshop
HIST2991.description: This seminar is for History PhD students in residence at Brown who are post-exams and are at any stage of writing their dissertations. It is intended to support dissertators by providing a structured community for setting and sharing goals, writing, and discussing chapters-in-progress. It meets every other week and is a half credit S/NC course.

HIST2992K.name: The Politics of Knowledge (STS 2000)
HIST2992K.description: Interested students must register for STS 2000.

HIST2992L.name: Race and Species: Beyond Hierarchies, Towards New Alliances (HMAN 2402Q)
HIST2992L.description: Interested students must register for HMAN 2402Q.

HIST2992M.name: Orthodoxy and Heresy in Islamic Thought RELS 2400A.
HIST2992M.description: Interested students must register for RELS 2400A.

HMAN0800C.name: Blue Humanities: Poetics That Unsettle the Oceanic Demise
HMAN0800C.description: Amidst the climate crisis, warming oceans demand collaborations across science and technology studies and histories of anti-imperialism. Shifting attention off dry land, “blue humanities” draw from multiple genres and disciplines to answer such questions as: How are oceanic flows transformed by climate change, capitalism, and empire? What narrative methods are suitable for understanding oceans that carry traces of refusal and survival? How do queer and Indigenous perspectives seep into water? Climate fiction, science and technology studies, and histories of resistance at sea will be examined through novels, poetry, ethnography, and film. We will experiment with writing through “submerged” and “wet" perspectives that potentially unsettle fixed categories. Approaching the environment from the sea, underwater, and offshore makes space for decolonial imaginations, queer ecologies, and more-than-human relations.

HMAN0900V.name: Family Studies: A Data Humanities Seminar
HMAN0900V.description: This course is framed by the recognition that big data and social analysis are efforts to scale that can obscure the humans who are documented, enumerated, and analyzed. In the course, we will think with ethnographies and histories of the causes and consequences of counting humans, paying special attention to the ethics of collecting, analyzing, and publishing data. To ground our exploration of the human side of data, we will focus on personally meaningful scholarship: as a hands-on project, each student will tackle an individually relevant data project from a humanistic perspective, centering on their experience of family, from genealogical records to family photo albums to oral histories to quilting. This course bridges theory and methodology, asking why we count what we count — and what we miss when we invest too much in the counting.

HMAN1000B.name: The Cogut Institute for the Humanities Research Seminar
HMAN1000B.description: This yearlong seminar involves reading and discussing in-progress research by the annual fellows of the Cogut Institute for the Humanities, an interdisciplinary group of faculty, postdoctoral fellows, graduate students, and undergraduates engaged in extended research on a major project or honors thesis. Students read a wide range of works-in-progress, prepare questions and participate in seminar discussions, serve as first questioners for specific sessions assigned to them in advance, and present their own work twice during the year. Students are required to complete both semesters (HMAN 1000A in the fall and HMAN 1000B in the spring) to receive credit. Admission to the course requires that students have received the Cogut Institute Undergraduate Fellowship for the year in which they enroll. More information about the fellowship and application process may be found at https://humanities.brown.edu/apply/undergraduate-fellowship.

HMAN1977S.name: Bottom Ecologies: Blackness, Queerness, and the Environment
HMAN1977S.description: How have Black queer communities — and minoritarian communities more broadly — transformed environments of shame and disposability into sources of erotic power, pleasure, and collective survival? Building on Toni Morrison’s “Sula” and theories from Black feminisms, queer-of-color critique, and Black ecological thought, this course views the “bottom” as Black queer ecological thought. We will trace how Black queer communities generate counter-knowledge, reshape racialized and sexual subjectivities, and challenge conventional environmental discourse by queering ecological analysis. Ultimately, this course examines the “bottom” as both a sexual position and an ecological site historically raced, and marked as disposable, dirty, abject. Readings from Morrison, Jennifer Nash, Audre Lorde, Darieck Scott, Juana María Rodríguez, Kathryn Bond Stockton, and Leo Bersani will guide our exploration of how landscapes of racial abjection and erotic desire converge, offering new critical tools for environmental humanities.

HMAN1977W.name: The History of Greater Latinx Los Angeles
HMAN1977W.description: This seminar explores the history of Greater Los Angeles as it relates to ethnic Latino/a/x/e populations. Comprising a population of over 18.5 million people, “Greater Los Angeles” describes the five counties in Southern California (Los Angeles, Orange County, San Bernardino, Riverside, and Ventura) that make up the second-largest metropolitan area in the United States and the third-largest metropolitan area in the world by nominal GDP, following only Tokyo and New York City. By reading and critically discussing classic and contemporary works in the field, along with an examination of documentary films and primary sources, students will explore the critical social, cultural, political, and economic roles that Latinos have had in shaping Greater Los Angeles. Major themes in the course are immigration, gentrification, race, ethnicity, urban inequality, place-making, community formation, and economic development.

HMAN1977X.name: Crafting Knowledge: Learning and Knowing in Ancient Egypt (3000–2000 BCE)
HMAN1977X.description: How did ancient Egyptians conceptualize, create, preserve, and transmit knowledge over 4,000 years ago, across a wide geographical space and in a world where communication methods were vastly different from today? This course examines the early Pharaonic history, with a particular focus on the third millennium BCE — a period marked by urbanization, institutional development, the emergence of one of the earliest writing systems, and the rise of complex social hierarchies. Through archaeological evidence and textual sources, we will reflect on notions of knowing and learning, including oral and written practices, from ritual knowledge to crafts, across different domains of society and regions. We will also investigate how knowledge was disseminated and preserved through institutions, technologies, and social structures, while reflecting on how modern scholarship constructs knowledge about the ancient past.

HMAN2300.name: Introduction to Digital Humanities
HMAN2300.description: Digital humanities uses digital methodologies and formats to answer humanities research questions, produce and share knowledge, and teach. It encompasses critical studies of digital environments, innovative modes of researching and advancing arguments (including methodologies for constituting archives, analyzing texts and images, and visualizing data), new forms of scholarly and general publications, and digital pedagogy. The digital changes the way we research, understand, and share information in the humanities. This course will introduce students to a range of methodologies and critical lenses. Students will learn to collect resources formatted for machine-actionable research, analyze qualitative and quantitative datasets, and visualize and present their findings. They will consider the ethics of digital work and publication. Each student will plan a digital humanities project. This course is open to all graduate students and fulfills a requirement for the doctoral certificate in digital humanities.

HMAN2402P.name: Universal Humanism?
HMAN2402P.description: This course is an exploration of the (im)possibilities of universal humanism as a political and ethical aspiration in the 21st century. This exploration centrally stages a conversation between some Western political thought and critical Black studies, though the dialectic extends to include thinking in animal studies, queer and feminist theory, postcolonialism, critical disability studies, Indigenous studies, critical ecology, deconstruction, psychoanalysis, affect theory, and new materialism. We will also think about how literariness — the idea of literacy, the methods of narrative and poetics — contributes to discourses of the human. Some primary interlocutors here will include Hannah Arendt, James Baldwin, Judith Butler, Lucille Clifton, Frantz Fanon, Michel Foucault, Emmanuel Levinas, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Toni Morrison, Hortense Spillers, Patricia Williams, and Sylvia Wynter. In brief, this course asks, can universal humanism be salvaged — and if so, on what grounds?

HMAN2402Q.name: Race and Species: Beyond Hierarchies, Towards New Alliances
HMAN2402Q.description: This seminar explores the historical and contemporary co-constitution of race and species. While these categories have existed and intersected since ancient times, we will concentrate on how differences were flattened into the hierarchies of life in European empires, racializing non-humans and animalizing colonized peoples. Beyond these historical prejudices, we will investigate the complex and often surprising intersections between these categories, in alliances, shared scholarly approaches, and evolving theories of agency. Through case studies and critical inquiry, we will challenge exclusionary concepts of the human. By engaging these frameworks to improve conceptions of social and environmental justice, this seminar offers a lens for understanding our interconnected world. In addition to reading assigned published works, participants will gain experience in a collaboration with an international set of authors and editors producing a planned volume on race and species.

HMAN2402R.name: The Origins and Afterlives of Ethnic Studies
HMAN2402R.description: This seminar traces ethnic studies from its political and intellectual origins in the late 1960s through its contemporary forms and futures. We will examine how the field has transformed academic disciplines, met institutional (and outside) resistance, and navigated scholarly debates about methods, boundaries, and commitments. Students will engage genealogies of key concepts and scholarly traditions while considering the broader stakes of engaged research in higher education. The seminar is intentionally collaborative: students will work together throughout—thinking, researching, and producing collective work—while reflecting on the efforts and challenges of those who established and sustained the field. Guest scholars will share diverse specializations and methods. Through collaborative projects and presentations, students will develop informed perspectives on ethnic studies' significance and relevance today.

HMAN2500.name: Project Development Workshop
HMAN2500.description: In this capstone course, students pursuing the Doctoral Certificates in Collaborative and Environmental Humanities elaborate individual or collaborative projects, such as a stand-alone component of a dissertation chapter, an article on method/theory, or an essay related to the larger field. The workshop comprises several stages of collaboration, involving assignments and exercises that culminate in a final public event. It provides a supportive space in which students from different disciplines can share their work. Emphasis is placed on developing a sense of one’s larger intellectual commitments and investments, and on learning to communicate one’s ideas and values in the context of a multidisciplinary audience. Attention is also paid to key forms of professionalization, including public speaking, crafting and responding to analytical questions, and audio/visual interviewing as a form of professional inquiry and self-presentation. Enrollment requires admission in either certificate.

HMAN2971K.name: Science and Knowledge (PHIL 2730)
HMAN2971K.description: Interested students must register for PHIL 2730.

HNDI0200.name: Beginning Hindi or Urdu
HNDI0200.description: Introduces conversation, reading, and writing of modern standard Hindi and the Devanagari script. Those who already know Devanagari but have rusty conversation skills may join the class second semester; obtain instructor's permission during the first semester. Those who prefer to learn Urdu and the Persian script should contact the instructor. Prerequisite: HNDI 0100.

HNDI0400.name: Intermediate Hindi-Urdu
HNDI0400.description: A continuation of HNDI 0100-0200. Introduces the variation of the Persian script used for Urdu. Prepares students to communicate in written and spoken language. Activities are conducted in Hindi/Urdu. Meets four hours weekly. Prerequisite: HNDI 0300.

HNDI1080.name: Advanced Hindi-Urdu
HNDI1080.description: Each student follows an independent reading list determined in consultation with the instructor. The readings may include folk tales, journalistic prose, 20th-century literature, classical Urdu poetry of the 17th to 19th centuries, or subjects in nonfiction. The class meets together three hours weekly for discussion. Each student also spends one hour weekly with the instructor. Prerequisite: HNDI 0400.

HSP0330.name: Health Law and Policy
HSP0330.description: PHP 0330 provides an overview of how law shapes the U.S. health care system, including key health policy aims of access, quality, affordability, and equity. “Health Law” includes the laws and public policies that apply to the health care system or affect health care delivery. Health law profoundly shapes the U.S. health care system and the health and welfare of the population. The law has an important role in advancing (or retrenching) health equity through enforcement of individual rights and structuring the distribution of resources within the society. This course will cover core health law topics, including the regulation of health insurance and financing, quality, competition, provider–patient relationships, reproductive health care, and antidiscrimination in health care. The course will surveying the historical development and existing health law and policy and apply policy evaluation frameworks to engage in policy analysis.

HSP0650.name: From Manufacturer to Patient:  Why is the Cost of Prescription Drugs So Darn High?
HSP0650.description: In 2015, estimates of drug spend in the United States was about $457 billion and could be as high as $610 billion by 2021. The reasons for the continued escalating costs of prescription drugs are unclear. In this course we will examine the complex chain of discounts, rebates and markups that impact the price of a prescription drug from the manufacturer’s list price to the time it is dispensed to the patient. We will examine the role of major stakeholders in the drug supply chain including the manufacturer, wholesalers and distributors, pharmacy benefit managers and health plans. PHP 0310, Healthcare in the United States, is a prerequisite. Students who feel they have adequate background and understanding of health insurance, Medicare and Medicaid and model of care delivery and financing but have not taken PHP 0310 should contact instructor for override.

HSP1100.name: Comparative Health Care Systems
HSP1100.description: Focuses on principles of national health system organization and cross-national comparative analysis. Emphasizes application of comparative models to the analysis of health and health-related systems across nations. Addresses research questions related to population health and systems' performance.

HSP1490.name: Methods in Health Economics and Policy
HSP1490.description: This course equips students with econometric tools to evaluate health programs and policies. Focusing on causal inference methods—such as randomized experiments, differences-in-differences, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, and synthetic controls—students learn to assess and design rigorous studies that inform public health decisions. Emphasis is placed on applying basic economic theory in real-world contexts and interpreting evidence for impact evaluation. Students will carry out a hands-on research project using statistical software to test a theory-driven hypothesis. By the end of the course, students will be prepared to contribute to evidence-based public health practice and policy evaluation. This course assumes prior exposure to basic regression and microeconomic concepts.

HSP1495.name: Introduction To Global Health Economics & Finance
HSP1495.description: This course provides an examination of the economic architecture and financial mechanisms that underpin health and healthcare in the Global South. Moving beyond basic theory, students critically analyze how financial flows, economic incentives, and market failures shape health outcomes in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).The course is divided into seven two-week modules. It begins with the macro-level evolving “architecture" of global health financing before drilling down into microeconomic principles, the dynamics of poverty, and specific disease burdens. A unique focus is the integration of behavioral economics —a key research area of the instructor— and how human behavior, economic incentives, and rational choice intersect with epidemiological models and outcomes.

HSP1500.name: Improving the Quality of Health Care: From Measurement to Action
HSP1500.description: The quality of health care in the United States is in urgent need of improvement. This course will focus on the science of measuring and improving the quality of health care. Topics will include quality assessment, patient safety, medical errors, public reporting, financial incentives, organizational change, and health care disparities. Students will engage in a team-based quality improvement project with a partnering health care organization.

HSP1585.name: Evidence and Public Policy
HSP1585.description: This course introduces students to the role of evidence in the public policy process. The goal is to enable students to understand how the use of evidence and research interacts with the political and normative considerations that shape public policy. It also aims to help students become more engaged participants in shaping and generating policy ideas. The course will cover topics such as what counts as “good” evidence and how evidence is shared with and disseminated to policymakers.

HSP1681.name: Reproductive Health, Rights and Justice
HSP1681.description: This course will explore how reproductive health, healthcare and freedom are regulated in the United States. The course will apply an reproductive justice framework that investigates laws, policies and practices affecting reproductive rights and bodily autonomy, but that also applies an intersectional lens to consider how race, gender, sexuality, class, ability, and immigration status affect reproduction and parenting for marginalized communities. We will also explore how religion and ideas of morality shape laws, policies and practices implicating reproductive health, bodily autonomy and notions of reproductive justice. Topics will include: eugenics, sterilization, contraception, abortion, criminal fetal endangerment laws, substance use during pregnancy, reproductive rights of incarcerated populations, access to reproductive healthcare, assisted reproduction, surrogacy, maternal health disparities, the child welfare system, and policies related to parenting and family health. Readings will include public health, law and policy analysis and landmark legal

HSP1682.name: Health, Functioning, and Disability in Aging
HSP1682.description:
Aging is one of the most important forces shaping our society, healthcare system, and economy. As people live longer than ever before, understanding how to support health, function, and quality of life in later years has become a central public health challenge.This course provides an overview of these issues with emphasis on the epidemiology of age-related health conditions and how they translate into functional limitations, disability, and participation in everyday life. It is organized into three modules: (1) major public health challenges of aging, (2) how function and disability are defined, measured, and experienced, and (3) the laws, services, and systems designed to support older adults.
Topics include conceptual frameworks of health function and disability, major types of functional limitations—physical, sensory, cognitive, and developmental—as well as common conditions associated with aging and the challenges faced by individuals with functional limitations.

HSP1684.name: What is an Ounce of Prevention Worth? The Evidence and Politics of Disease Prevention in the US
HSP1684.description: It is said, “An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.”  But when it comes to our health, is that what the evidence really says?  Preventive care accounts for over half of all primary care visits in the US; yet, what constitutes effective preventive care is controversial.  In this course, students will learn the scientific underpinnings of disease prevention and how prevention strategies get translated into policy and practice – to both the benefit and detriment of the American population. The course will illustrate key concepts such as primary and secondary prevention; pre-clinical disease; intermediate and health outcomes; and overdiagnosis. Students will engage with theoretical readings and use-cases of key prevention strategies. The class will emphasize practical experiences, including deliberations on topics reviewed by the US Preventive Services Task Force, mock press conferences, and presentations to practicing physicians.

HSP2077A.name: Capstone: Policy Brief
HSP2077A.description:
The Integrated Learning Experience (ILE) is designed to enable MPH students to synthesize learning across their core courses, concentration courses, and practicum experiences. Historically, the Brown School of Public Health has required a thesis for the ILE, however, students may now complete a thesis or a capstone course as their ILE. The thesis is the better option for those who want to conduct academic research with a mentor in an independent study-type format, the capstone course is for those who prefer an applied project in a classroom setting.
Policy Brief: Students who choose to enroll in the policy brief section will learn to examine policy options to address emerging issues, analyze the possibilities, and communicate recommendations as a policy brief. Students will design their brief to provide decision makers with analysis-based recommendations on a specific issue or problem.

HSP2400.name: The U.S. Health Care System: Case Studies in Financing, Delivery, Regulation and Public Health
HSP2400.description: Reviews the development of the health care delivery, financing and regulatory control systems in the U.S. and reviews the literature on the relationship between health system structure and the services used and health outcomes that populations experience. A case-study approach is used to understand the inter-relationship between financing, delivery and regulatory components of the health system and their implication for public health by drawing on epidemiological, economic, political and sociological principals. Prerequisites: Graduate standing or PHP 0310 and instructor permission.

HSP2411.name: Introduction to Health Policy Analysis
HSP2411.description: In this course, students will learn about historical and contemporary state and federal health policies and the methods used to evaluate their efficacy, with a major focus on the Medicare program. Students will learn how to use statistical analysis software to manage and analyze real Medicare claims data, which are the main data source for landmark health services research studies.

HSP2455B.name: Health Services Research Methods II
HSP2455B.description:
Health services researchers use theories, models, and data to understand the health care system, assess the effectiveness of interventions (at multiple levels of the healthcare system), and inform health policy decisions. This course reviews the application of statistical and epidemiological principles to the design and analysis of health services research studies with a focus on causal inference methods. Methods and topics we will cover include panel data designs, difference-in-difference, synthetic controls, GEE, random and fixed effects, survival analysis, missing data, IV, propensity scores, research ethics, and statistical methods to study equity.
This doctoral level course is the continuation of PHP2455A, and students are recommended to take both in sequence, however students with sufficient epidemiologic or econometric training may enroll with instructor permission.

IAPA0300.name: Costs of War
IAPA0300.description: This interdisciplinary seminar explores a ground-level view of war and its human, economic, environmental, and social consequences. We primarily take up the example of the post-9/11 wars, focusing less on the causes of war, on battles, elite war strategies, or relations between states than on what war is like for those caught within it, what larger social and economic contexts make it more or less likely, what are its impacts for many differently situated peoples, and how myths about violence, and even the category of war itself, often obscures fuller understanding.

IAPA0310.name: Reimagining Human Security
IAPA0310.description: The concept of human security– in both theory and practice– has significantly evolved over the past two decades, with the idea that people, and the protection of human life and dignity, should be the central focus of governmental and intergovernmental security policy and practice. Yet, despite many advances in the field, the world is more dangerous than ever, and vulnerable civilians are increasingly threatened by a multitude of challenges including war, climate change, pandemics, natural disasters, the erosion of humanitarian and human rights law, and rapid advances in world-changing technologies. How do global issues such as climate change, pandemics, artificial intelligence, and migration impact human security? In what ways do social, economic, environmental, and political factors intersect in the context of human security? What ethical considerations should be considered when reimagining approaches to human security?

IAPA1001.name: Foundations of Development
IAPA1001.description: This course presents an interdisciplinary approach to the study of development. The course examines what constitutes development from a variety of different disciplinary perspectives, and the course examines how and in what context the term “development” itself has evolved over time. The goal of this course is to provide students an intellectual and conceptual grounding for study a variety of issues surrounding development, whether in the global North or South.

IAPA1201E.name: Nonprofit Organizations
IAPA1201E.description: Contemporary nonprofits and their role in community building and shaping public policy are central to this course. Topics include how strong coalitions impact housing, welfare and children's policy, organizing empowered communities, the influential and engaged donor and building the value of nonprofits. Case studies will be featured and new nonprofit models will be conceptualized to strategically address critical human need. Enrollment limited to 20 juniors, seniors, and graduate students concentrating in Public Policy. This course satisfies the American Institutions requirement.

IAPA1500D.name: Research Design and Methods
IAPA1500D.description: This course provides an introduction to research design in the social sciences. The goals of the course are two-fold: to instruct students to critically analyze scholarly articles in terms of research design and to guide students in designing an original research project. The methods presented in the course include qualitative methods (e.g., interviews, focus groups, participant observation, and process tracing) and quantitative methods (e.g., surveys, observational studies, and experiments).  The course is designed as preparation for a senior thesis or original research project. All assignments in the course revolve around the development of an original research project. The research itself will not be conducted as part of the course. There are no prerequisites for the course and a background in statistics is not required.

IAPA1702P.name: State and Nation Building in Communist and Post Communist Europe
IAPA1702P.description: This seminar investigates the politics of state-building and nation-building in communist and post-communist Eastern Europe since World War I. The course is designed as a Junior Seminar for the IAPA concentration, and its major requirement is the writing of a 25-to-30-page research paper on a subject of the student’s choosing (Capstone Project). Ideally, students will come to the course with some idea of a problem or question that the want to spend the better part of the semester researching. The seminar, however, is open anybody with a demonstrated interest in the region and who is ready to read and seriously discuss texts drawn from a wide range of vocations –from literature and politics, to history, philosophy, economics, sociology, political science, and public policy.

IAPA1702T.name: Technology and Development
IAPA1702T.description: With the most recent inventions, a “smart” global order is being created, where information and communication technologies (ICT) dominate public arenas and private lives. Most of the debates on new technologies still focus on the Global North, yet the impact on the Global South may be at least as significant. In this seminar, we will explore the history, present, and possible futures of the use of technologies for transforming economic, social and political lives. The technologies discussed will range from the steam power central to the 19th century industrial revolution to today’s mobile phone technologies, workforce automation, and facial-recognition technologies.

IAPA1800D.name: Introduction to Corporate Law and Public Policy
IAPA1800D.description: This course will give students an introduction to business organizations – the law that governs corporations and partnerships, how they raise money in the financial markets, and to explore the public policy issues that inform the regulation of business and finance.  We will look at business organizations,  law that governs how companies raise money, operation of the stock markets, insider trading, and the regulation of institutional investors including mutual funds, hedge funds and private equity funds.  We will finish by taking up corporations as persons, their social obligations and the recent Supreme Court cases on corporations and the First Amendment. Overrides granted based on random drawing for 11 seniors and 8 juniors; to be eligible you must turn in the first week’s assignment and attend the first class.  Put course in your cart to access the assignment via canvas.

IAPA1801D.name: Politics & Journalism: A Practical Guide to How We Got Here and Where We’re Going
IAPA1801D.description: Politics in America has never been so manic, so divided, so pervasive, so vital. But we’re not just in overlapping crises of government and democracy and economics and race. We’re also in a crisis of truth. It’s impossible to think about what is happening in politics without thinking about how it’s covered. This course will explore that connection—in a practice-oriented, writing intensive approach which will aim to transform your understanding both of what’s really happening in politics and how those developments are presented to the public. Fulfills IAPA senior capstone/seminar requirement.

IAPA1801Y.name: The Politics of Regulation: Technology, Finance, and Climate Change
IAPA1801Y.description: Technological innovations are a central force for economic development, but today we are facing some of their most severe and unintended consequences.  Some observers argue that only market competition can enable the blossoming of human ingenuity, while others argue that state planning is essential for controlling the dangers inherent in new technologies.  Rather than extol or deny the benefits that can come from technology, this course examines how governments in different historical circumstances have attempted to shape and regulate three of the most challenging risks facing advanced societies.

IAPA1802M.name: Rwanda Past and Present
IAPA1802M.description: In the mid-1990s, few countries on earth were as devastated as Rwanda.  As many as one million people or more had been killed in a 100-day genocide, and the fleeing regime had left the country in ruins.  Today, however, Rwanda is not only at peace but full of ambition.
